questions.stem: Which type of data is tumour stage (I, II, III, IV)?
questions.explanation: Tumour stage is ordinal categorical — categories have a meaningful order (I < II < III < IV) but the intervals between stages are not equal.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of continuous numerical data?
questions.explanation: Serum creatinine is continuous — it can take any value on a continuum. Lymph node count is discrete. Blood group is nominal. ECOG and cancer stage are ordinal.

questions.stem: What is the key difference between interval and ratio data?
options: Interval data has no true zero
questions.explanation: Interval data (e.g., temperature in °C) has equal intervals but no true zero — 0°C does not mean 'no temperature.' Ratio data (e.g., height, weight, dose) has a true zero, allowing ratio comparisons (200 cm is twice 100 cm).

questions.stem: Classify the following variables by data type: (a) Number of hospital admissions, (b) Blood group, (c) Pain score (0–10), (d) Height in cm.
questions.correct_answer: (a) Discrete numerical. (b) Nominal categorical. (c) Ordinal categorical. (d) Continuous numerical (ratio).
questions.explanation: Counting produces discrete data. Categories without order are nominal. Ordered categories with unequal intervals are ordinal. Measurements on a continuum are continuous.

questions.stem: A researcher records the number of metastatic sites in 50 patients. This variable is best described as:
questions.explanation: Number of metastatic sites is discrete numerical — it can only take integer values (0, 1, 2, ...). It is not continuous (cannot be 1.5 metastases).

questions.stem: For a dataset with positive skew, which is true?
questions.explanation: In positive (right) skew, the tail pulls the mean to the right, so mean > median. Examples: survival times, PSA levels, length of hospital stay.

questions.stem: Which measure of central tendency is most appropriate for ordinal data?
questions.explanation: Median is appropriate for ordinal data because it uses only the ordering of values. Mean requires equal intervals, which ordinal data lacks.

questions.stem: In a normal distribution, approximately what percentage of values lie within ±2 standard deviations of the mean?
questions.explanation: Within ±1 SD: 68%. ±1.96 SD (approx ±2): 95%. ±2.58 SD: 99%. ±3 SD: 99.7%. The exact value for ±2 is ~95.4% but with the common approximation it's 95%.

questions.stem: The coefficient of variation is calculated as:
questions.explanation: CV = (SD / mean) × 100%. It allows comparison of variability between datasets with different units or means (e.g., comparing BMI variability to blood pressure variability).

questions.stem: A dataset: 2, 4, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12, 15. Calculate the median and IQR.
questions.correct_answer: Median = 7 (5th of 9 ordered values). Q1 = 4 (median of lower half: 2,4,4,5). Q3 = 10 (median of upper half: 8,10,12,15). IQR = 10 − 4 = 6.
questions.explanation: For an odd number of observations, the median is the middle value. Q1 is median of values below the overall median; Q3 is median of values above.

questions.stem: A z-score of +1.96 corresponds to which percentile in the standard normal distribution?
questions.explanation: z = 1.96 is the 97.5th percentile. This means 2.5% of values lie above it, and since the distribution is symmetric, 95% lie between z = −1.96 and z = +1.96.

questions.stem: The Central Limit Theorem states that:
options: The population distribution becomes normal as n increases
The sampling distribution of the mean approaches normality as n increases
The sample variance equals the population variance for large n
The median equals the mean for large samples
The standard error equals the standard deviation for large n
questions.explanation: The CLT states that the sampling distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution as sample size increases, regardless of the underlying population distribution. This justifies parametric tests for n ≥ 30.

questions.stem: In a population with mean μ = 100 and SD σ = 15, what is the z-score for a value of 130?
questions.correct_answer: z = (130 − 100) / 15 = 30 / 15 = 2.0. This value is 2 standard deviations above the mean.
questions.explanation: The z-score standardises values: z = (x − μ) / σ. z = 2 corresponds to the ~97.7th percentile.

questions.stem: When is the t-distribution used instead of the normal distribution for confidence intervals?
options: When the sample size is large (n > 100)
When the population SD is unknown and n is small
When the data is positively skewed
When comparing more than two groups
questions.explanation: The t-distribution is used when σ is unknown and must be estimated from the sample (using s). It has fatter tails than the normal, producing wider CIs to account for the additional uncertainty. As n increases, t approaches z.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for the mean difference between two treatments is (−0.5, 3.2). What does this mean?
options: There is a 95% chance the true difference is between −0.5 and 3.2
The difference is not statistically significant at α = 0.05
The treatment is effective with 95% certainty
95% of patients have a difference between −0.5 and 3.2
questions.explanation: The CI includes zero (the null value for a difference), so the result is not significant at α = 0.05 (p > 0.05). Answer A is incorrect — a CI does not give the probability of the true value being in the interval.

questions.stem: If the sample size increases while all else stays the same, the width of a 95% CI will:
options: Increase if n < 30, decrease if n ≥ 30
questions.explanation: CI = mean ± t × (s/√n). As n increases, √n increases → SEM = s/√n decreases → CI narrows. Larger samples give more precise estimates.

questions.stem: A study of 100 patients reports mean tumour volume = 45 cm³, SD = 20 cm³. Calculate the 95% CI for the mean.
questions.explanation: With n = 100 (large), we can use z = 1.96 for the 95% CI. For smaller samples, we would use the t-distribution. The CI tells us the range of plausible values for the true population mean.

questions.stem: A p-value is defined as:
options: The probability that the null hypothesis is true
The probability of the observed data assuming the null hypothesis is true
The probability of observing the data (or more extreme) assuming H₀ is true
The probability that the alternative hypothesis is false
The probability of a Type II error
questions.explanation: The p-value is P(data or more extreme | H₀). It is NOT the probability that H₀ is true (which is a Bayesian concept). This is a frequently tested distinction.

questions.stem: A Type I error occurs when:
options: H₀ is false and we fail to reject it
H₀ is true and we reject it
H₀ is false and we correctly reject it
H₀ is true and we fail to reject it
The sample size is too small
questions.explanation: Type I error = false positive — rejecting H₀ when it is true. Probability = α (significance level, typically 0.05). Type II error = failing to reject false H₀. Power = 1 − β = correctly rejecting false H₀.

questions.stem: Study power depends on all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Direction of the alternative hypothesis (one- vs two-tailed)
questions.explanation: Power is a pre-study concept (calculated at design stage). It depends on effect size, sample size, α, variability, and test direction. The observed p-value is a result, not a determinant of power. Post-hoc power calculations are invalid.

questions.stem: A study reports p = 0.08 comparing a new drug to placebo. What can you conclude?
questions.correct_answer: With α = 0.05, p = 0.08 > 0.05, so the result is NOT statistically significant. There is insufficient evidence to reject H₀. However, this does NOT prove the drug is ineffective — the study may be underpowered. Look at the CI to see the range of plausible effects.
questions.explanation: Common FRCR trap: p > 0.05 ≠ 'no difference.' It means 'insufficient evidence to conclude a difference exists.' A small study with a large true effect can still give p > 0.05.

questions.stem: What is the relationship between a 95% CI excluding the null value and the p-value?
questions.correct_answer: If a 95% CI excludes the null value (0 for differences, 1 for RR/OR), then p < 0.05. Conversely, if the CI includes the null value, p > 0.05. The CI and p-value are consistent in the Neyman-Pearson framework.
questions.explanation: This is why CIs are often preferred — they show both significance AND the range of plausible effect sizes.

questions.stem: An independent t-test is most appropriate when:
options: Comparing before-and-after measurements in the same patients
Comparing two independent groups on a continuous outcome
Comparing three or more treatment groups
questions.explanation: Independent t-test: two independent groups, continuous (normally distributed) outcome. Paired t-test: before/after. ANOVA: ≥3 groups. Chi-square: proportions. Correlation: association.

questions.stem: A paired t-test has how many degrees of freedom?
questions.explanation: Paired t-test: df = n − 1, where n = number of pairs. Independent t-test (equal variances): df = n₁ + n₂ − 2. One-sample t-test: df = n − 1.

questions.stem: Explain when to use Welch's t-test instead of Student's t-test.
questions.correct_answer: Welch's t-test does not assume equal variances between groups. Use it when Levene's test shows significant variance heterogeneity (p < 0.05). Welch's test adjusts the degrees of freedom downward (Satterthwaite approximation). Most modern statistical software uses Welch's t-test as default.
questions.explanation: Student's t-test assumes equal variances. If violated, the Type I error rate is inflated. Welch's t-test is robust to variance differences and is recommended even when variances are equal.

questions.stem: What is the degrees of freedom for a chi-square test of independence on a 3 × 4 contingency table?
When is Fisher's exact test preferred over chi-square?
options: When the total sample size is > 100
When more than 20% of expected frequencies are < 5
When there are more than 2 rows
questions.explanation: Fisher's exact test is used when chi-square assumptions are violated — particularly when expected frequencies are small. The rule: no more than 20% of expecteds < 5, and none < 1.

questions.stem: McNemar's test is used when:
options: Testing correlation between two continuous variables
questions.explanation: McNemar's test is for paired categorical data (e.g., same patients before and after treatment). It only analyses discordant pairs and ignores concordant pairs. Example: testing if a new method detects more lesions than the standard method.

questions.stem: In a 2 × 2 table with a = 30, b = 10, c = 20, d = 40, calculate the chi-square statistic (without Yates' correction).
questions.explanation: Chi-square tests whether the observed frequencies differ significantly from expected under independence. A large χ² indicates a strong association.

questions.stem: One-way ANOVA compares:
questions.explanation: One-way ANOVA tests whether means of ≥ 3 independent groups are equal. F = MSB / MSW. If ANOVA is significant, post-hoc tests (Bonferroni, Tukey) identify which groups differ.

questions.stem: If a one-way ANOVA is significant (p < 0.05), what should you do next?
options: Remove the group with the highest mean
questions.explanation: A significant ANOVA tells you at least one group differs, but not which ones. Post-hoc tests (Bonferroni, Tukey, Scheffé) adjust for multiple comparisons to identify specific group differences.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of one-way ANOVA?
options: Equal sample sizes in all groups
questions.explanation: ANOVA does NOT require equal sample sizes, though unbalanced designs have reduced power. Assumptions: independence, normality of residuals, homogeneity of variances (Levene's test). If variances are unequal, use Welch's ANOVA.

questions.stem: The Mann-Whitney U test is the non-parametric equivalent of:
questions.explanation: Mann-Whitney U (Wilcoxon rank-sum) = non-parametric equivalent of independent t-test. Wilcoxon signed-rank = paired t-test. Kruskal-Wallis = one-way ANOVA.

questions.stem: When should Spearman's rank correlation be used instead of Pearson's?
options: When the relationship is non-linear but monotonic
When comparing more than two groups
When sample size is less than 10
questions.explanation: Spearman's ρ measures monotonic (not necessarily linear) relationships using ranks. Use it when data is non-normal, ordinal, or the relationship is non-linear but consistently increasing/decreasing.

questions.stem: Name the non-parametric alternative to one-way ANOVA and the test used for repeated measures ANOVA.
questions.correct_answer: Kruskal-Wallis test (for ≥3 independent groups, non-parametric alternative to one-way ANOVA). Friedman test (non-parametric alternative to repeated measures ANOVA).
questions.explanation: Both tests work on ranks. Kruskal-Wallis compares mean ranks across groups. Friedman test compares ranks within matched sets.

questions.stem: Which non-parametric test is the alternative to the paired t-test?
questions.explanation: The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is used for paired/related samples when the differences are not normally distributed. It ranks the absolute differences and sums ranks for positive and negative differences separately.

questions.stem: Pearson correlation coefficient r = 0 means:
options: There is a strong negative linear relationship
There is no linear relationship between the variables
The slope of the regression line is zero
questions.explanation: r = 0 means NO LINEAR relationship. However, there could still be a non-linear relationship (e.g., U-shaped). The regression slope β₁ = 0 when r = 0. Variables could still be associated non-linearly.

questions.stem: In simple linear regression, the coefficient of determination R² = 0.64 means:
options: 64% of the variance in y is explained by x
The correlation between x and y is 0.64
The regression model is statistically significant
64% of the data points lie on the regression line
questions.explanation: R² = proportion of variance in the outcome explained by the predictor(s). r = √0.64 = 0.80 (if slope positive). R² does not guarantee significance; it does not tell us about individual data points.

questions.stem: Which LINE assumption of linear regression is checked using a plot of residuals vs fitted values?
questions.explanation: Residuals vs fitted plot checks LINEARITY (no pattern = linear relationship holds) and HOMOSCEDASTICITY (constant spread = equal variance). A funnel shape indicates heteroscedasticity. Normality is checked with Q-Q plot. Independence is assumed from study design.

questions.stem: What is multicollinearity and how is it detected?
options: When predictors are highly correlated; VIF > 10
When residuals are non-normal; Shapiro-Wilk test
When the outcome has high variance; Levene's test
When there is interaction between predictors; ANOVA
questions.explanation: Multicollinearity = high correlation between predictors in multiple regression. This inflates standard errors of regression coefficients, making estimates unstable and hard to interpret. Detected by Variance Inflation Factor (VIF > 10 indicates serious collinearity).

questions.stem: A linear regression of tumour volume (cm³) on time (months) gives: volume = 10 + 8.5 × time. Interpret the slope and intercept.
questions.correct_answer: Intercept = 10 cm³: the estimated tumour volume at time 0 (baseline). Slope = 8.5 cm³/month: the tumour volume increases by an average of 8.5 cm³ per month. The intercept is interpretable here because time = 0 is meaningful (start of study).
questions.explanation: Regression coefficients describe the predicted change in outcome per unit change in predictor. The intercept is only meaningful when x = 0 is within the range of the data.

questions.stem: Logistic regression models the:
questions.explanation: Logistic regression models log(p/(1−p)) = β₀ + β₁x₁ + ... . The coefficients are log(OR). Exponentiating gives OR = exp(βᵢ). The probability P = 1 / (1 + exp(−(β₀ + β₁x₁ + ...))).

questions.stem: In logistic regression, the coefficient β = 1.2 for treatment (1 = new drug, 0 = standard). The odds ratio is:
questions.explanation: OR = exp(β) = e^1.2 ≈ 3.32. This means the odds of the outcome with the new drug are 3.32 times the odds with standard treatment. The coefficient β is the log(OR).

questions.stem: What is the proportional odds assumption in ordinal logistic regression?
questions.correct_answer: The proportional odds assumption states that the effect of each predictor on the log-odds of being at or above any threshold is the same across all thresholds. In other words, the OR comparing categories is constant regardless of which cut-point is used. Tested by the Brant test or score test.
questions.explanation: If violated, consider a partial proportional odds model or multinomial logistic regression (which does not assume ordered categories).

questions.stem: In a cohort study: 50/200 exposed develop disease vs 20/200 unexposed. The relative risk is:
questions.explanation: Risk(exposed) = 50/200 = 0.25. Risk(unexposed) = 20/200 = 0.10. RR = 0.25/0.10 = 2.5. Exposed individuals have 2.5 times the risk of developing disease compared to unexposed.

questions.stem: When is the odds ratio a good approximation of the relative risk?
options: When the sample size is large (>1000)
When the odds ratio is close to 1
When the study is a randomised trial
questions.explanation: OR ≈ RR when the outcome is rare (<10% prevalence). For common outcomes, OR exaggerates the effect compared to RR. This is called the 'rare disease assumption.'

questions.stem: A study reports OR = 0.45 (95% CI: 0.28–0.72) for the effect of a new screening programme on cancer mortality. The correct interpretation is:
options: The screening programme reduces odds of cancer death by 55%
The screening programme reduces risk of cancer death by 45%
The screening programme increases risk of cancer death by 45%
The result is not statistically significant
questions.explanation: OR = 0.45 means 55% reduction in odds (1 − 0.45 = 0.55). The CI (0.28–0.72) excludes 1, so it is significant. We cannot say 'risk' decrease without knowing baseline risk. NNT requires absolute risk, not OR.

questions.stem: Calculate NNT from the following: risk in control group = 0.20, risk in treatment group = 0.12.
questions.correct_answer: ARR = 0.20 − 0.12 = 0.08 = 8%. NNT = 1/ARR = 1/0.08 = 12.5. Round up → NNT = 13. You need to treat 13 patients to prevent one adverse outcome.
questions.explanation: NNT is clinically intuitive. Lower NNT = more effective treatment. NNT of 1 means every patient benefits. The 'Number Needed to Harm' (NNH) uses the same formula for adverse events.

questions.stem: Sensitivity is defined as:
questions.explanation: Sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN). 'Snout' — a highly Sensitive test rules OUT disease (negative result rules it out). Specificity = TN / (TN + FP) — 'Spin' — rules IN disease.

questions.stem: PPV depends on all of the following EXCEPT:
options: All of the above affect PPV
questions.explanation: PPV depends on sensitivity, specificity, and prevalence. Sample size does NOT directly affect PPV (though it affects precision of the estimate). PPV = (sens × prev) / (sens × prev + (1−spec) × (1−prev)).

questions.stem: A test has sensitivity 95% and specificity 90%. Disease prevalence is 2%. What is the PPV?
questions.explanation: In 10,000 people: 200 have disease (2%). TP = 190 (95% of 200). FP = 980 (10% of 9,800). PPV = 190/(190+980) = 190/1170 ≈ 16.2%. Despite high sens/spec, PPV is low because prevalence is low.

questions.stem: Calculate LR+ for a test with sensitivity 90% and specificity 85%.
questions.correct_answer: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 − specificity) = 0.90 / (1 − 0.85) = 0.90 / 0.15 = 6.0. A positive test is 6 times more likely in diseased than non-diseased patients. This moderately increases post-test probability.
questions.explanation: LR+ > 10: strong diagnostic evidence. LR+ 5–10: moderate. LR+ 2–5: weak. LR+ ~1: useless. LR− < 0.1: strong evidence to rule out disease.

questions.stem: On an ROC curve, the optimal diagnostic cut-off is usually at the point:
questions.explanation: The optimal cut-off maximises sensitivity + specificity (Youden's index = sensitivity + specificity − 1). This is the point closest to the top-left corner of the ROC curve. The AUC summarises overall test performance across all cut-offs.

questions.stem: What does AUC = 0.5 mean on an ROC curve?
questions.correct_answer: AUC = 0.5 means the test performs no better than random chance. The ROC curve lies along the diagonal line. AUC = 1.0 is a perfect test. Clinically useful tests typically have AUC ≥ 0.75.

questions.stem: Censoring in survival analysis occurs when:
options: A patient dies from the disease
A patient is lost to follow-up before the event occurs
All patients have experienced the event
questions.explanation: Censoring = patient leaves the study without experiencing the event (lost to follow-up, alive at study end, withdraws consent). Survival analysis methods (KM, Cox) correctly handle censored data. Censoring must be non-informative.

questions.stem: The log-rank test is used to:
questions.explanation: The log-rank test compares the entire survival distribution between two (or more) groups. It tests H₀: no difference in survival. It calculates observed vs expected events at each time point across groups.

questions.stem: A Cox proportional hazards model gives HR = 0.65 (95% CI 0.48–0.88) for a new treatment. The proportional hazards assumption:
options: Is automatically satisfied if the HR is significant
Means the survival curves are parallel
Means the hazard ratio is constant over time
Can be ignored for large samples
Is tested by the log-rank test
questions.explanation: Proportional hazards: the HR is constant over time. Checked by log(−log(survival)) plots (should be parallel) or Schoenfeld residuals test. If violated, use stratified Cox or time-dependent covariates.

questions.stem: Calculate the Kaplan-Meier survival probability at 12 months given: 20 patients start. Events at months 4 (2 events), 8 (1 event), 10 (1 event). Censored at month 6 (1 patient) and month 11 (2 patients). What is S(12)?
questions.explanation: KM estimate = cumulative product of conditional survival probabilities. The curve only drops at event times. Censored patients are removed from the at-risk set but not counted as events.

questions.stem: If median survival cannot be estimated from a Kaplan-Meier curve, this means:
options: More than 50% of patients are still alive at the end of follow-up
The log-rank test will be non-significant
The proportional hazards assumption is violated
questions.explanation: Median survival = time when S(t) = 0.5. If the KM curve never drops to 0.5 (i.e., >50% survival at last follow-up), median survival cannot be reported. This is common with good prognosis or short follow-up.

questions.stem: If the minimum clinically important difference is halved, the required sample size:
questions.explanation: Sample size is inversely proportional to the square of the effect size: n ∝ 1/δ². Halving δ requires 4× the sample size. This relationship highlights the challenge of detecting small effects.

questions.stem: Increasing power from 0.80 to 0.90 has what effect on required sample size?
questions.explanation: Increasing power from 0.80 (Zβ = 0.84) to 0.90 (Zβ = 1.28) increases (Zα/₂ + Zβ)² from (1.96 + 0.84)² = 7.84 to (1.96 + 1.28)² = 10.50. Ratio 10.50/7.84 ≈ 1.34, so ~34% more patients.

questions.stem: Why is 'post-hoc power' considered misleading?
questions.correct_answer: Post-hoc power calculates the power to detect the observed effect size, given the study's sample size. Since the observed effect is known, the calculation is circular. A non-significant result (p > 0.05) will always correspond to low 'post-hoc power.' It adds no information beyond the p-value and CI. Power should be calculated at the DESIGN stage, not after results are known.
questions.explanation: Some journals discourage reporting post-hoc power. Reporting the 95% CI for the effect size is more informative — it shows the range of effects compatible with the data.

questions.stem: If 10 independent tests are performed, each at α = 0.05, the family-wise error rate is approximately:
questions.explanation: FWER = 1 − (1 − α)^m = 1 − (0.95)^10 = 1 − 0.599 = 0.401. So there is a ~40% chance of at least one Type I error across 10 tests. Bonferroni correction: α-adjusted = 0.05/10 = 0.005 for each test.

questions.stem: The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure controls:
options: The probability of at least one Type I error
questions.explanation: Benjamini-Hochberg controls the FDR — the expected proportion of false discoveries among all rejected hypotheses. It is less conservative than FWER methods (Bonferroni) and is preferred in genomics and exploratory analyses where many hypotheses are tested.

questions.stem: What is the Bonferroni correction for 5 comparisons?
questions.correct_answer: Adjusted α = 0.05 / 5 = 0.01. Each individual test is considered significant only if p < 0.01.
questions.explanation: Bonferroni is the most conservative correction (highest Type II error rate). Use when tests are pre-specified and few. For many tests, FDR control is preferred.

questions.stem: The main purpose of randomisation in clinical trials is to:
options: Ensure equal numbers in each group
questions.explanation: Randomisation balances BOTH known and unknown confounders between groups. Stratification only balances known confounders. Blinding reduces measurement bias. Randomisation does not guarantee equal group sizes (though block randomisation can help).
questions.source_topic_reference: FRCR Medical Statistics — Clinical Trial Design

questions.stem: Intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis:
options: Analyses patients who completed the treatment as allocated
Analyses patients as randomised regardless of actual treatment received
Includes only patients with complete data
Analyses patients who received the intended treatment
questions.explanation: ITT = analyse as randomised, regardless of compliance, crossover, or withdrawal. It preserves the benefits of randomisation and estimates real-world effectiveness. Per-protocol analysis may overestimate efficacy.
questions.source_topic_reference: FRCR Medical Statistics — Clinical Trial Design

questions.stem: A non-inferiority trial aims to show that:
options: The new treatment is better than the standard
The new treatment is equivalent to the standard
The new treatment is not worse than the standard by more than a pre-specified margin
The new treatment has fewer side effects
questions.explanation: Non-inferiority: H₀: new < control − δ. Reject H₀ to show new is not worse than control by more than δ (the non-inferiority margin). Equivalence: |new − control| < δ. Superiority: new > control.
questions.source_topic_reference: FRCR Medical Statistics — Clinical Trial Design

questions.stem: What is double-blinding and why is it important?
questions.correct_answer: Double-blinding: neither the patient nor the investigator/assessor knows which treatment the patient is receiving. It minimises performance bias (patients may behave differently if they know their treatment) and detection bias (assessors may subconsciously influence outcome measurement).
questions.explanation: Triple-blinding also blinds the statistician. Blinding is not always possible (e.g., surgery vs medical treatment), but it should be maintained whenever feasible.
questions.source_topic_reference: FRCR Medical Statistics — Clinical Trial Design

questions.stem: What is the difference between a parallel group and a crossover trial?
questions.correct_answer: Parallel: each patient receives only one treatment. Groups are compared at the end. Crossover: each patient receives both treatments sequentially (with washout). Each patient acts as their own control — more powerful but requires no carry-over effect and stable disease.
questions.source_topic_reference: FRCR Medical Statistics — Clinical Trial Design

questions.stem: Confounding occurs when:
options: The effect of exposure differs across levels of another variable
A third variable is associated with both exposure and outcome, distorting the association
Two variables are highly correlated in a regression model
The outcome is measured with error
The sample is not representative of the population
questions.explanation: Confounding = a third variable (confounder) associated with BOTH exposure and outcome. Example: age confounds the relationship between grey hair and mortality (age causes both). Controlled by randomisation, stratification, or multivariate adjustment.

questions.stem: The ecological fallacy is:
options: Assuming individual-level associations apply at group level
Assuming group-level associations apply at individual level
Using the wrong statistical test for the data type
questions.explanation: Ecological fallacy = inferring individual-level relationships from group-level data. Example: areas with more immigrants have higher crime rates → 'immigrants commit more crime' is the fallacy. The group-level association may not hold at the individual level.

questions.stem: Simpson's paradox is best described as:
options: A trend appears in several groups but disappears or reverses when groups are combined
Extreme values become less extreme on re-measurement
Effect modification by a third variable
A Type I error due to multiple testing
questions.explanation: Simpson's paradox: a trend appears in separate groups but reverses when combined due to a confounding variable. Classic example: Berkeley sex bias case — each department admitted men and women at similar rates, but overall rates showed apparent bias against women because women applied to more competitive departments.

questions.stem: What is regression to the mean and why does it matter in clinical research?
questions.correct_answer: Regression to the mean: when a measurement is extreme on first assessment, it tends to be closer to the population mean on re-measurement. This matters because uncontrolled before/after studies (e.g., giving treatment to patients with highest blood pressure) will show apparent 'improvement' even with a placebo, simply due to this statistical phenomenon. This is why control groups are essential.
questions.explanation: FRCR exam trap: a study shows 'treatment lowers blood pressure' using before/after measurements without a control group. The apparent effect may be partly (or wholly) due to regression to the mean.

questions.stem: What is the difference between confounding and effect modification?
questions.correct_answer: Confounding distorts the exposure-outcome relationship and is controlled by adjustment. Effect modification (interaction) means the effect differs across subgroups — it is a finding to be reported, not controlled. Example: treatment may be effective in men but not women (effect modification by sex).

questions.stem: Publication bias in a meta-analysis is best detected by:
questions.explanation: Funnel plot: plot effect size (x-axis) vs precision/SE (y-axis, inverted). Asymmetric funnel suggests publication bias (missing small negative studies). Forest plot shows individual study results. I² measures heterogeneity. Funnel plot asymmetry can also be caused by heterogeneity.

questions.stem: The appropriate measure for comparing variability between datasets with different units is:
questions.explanation: CV = (SD/mean) × 100% is unitless and allows comparison of variability across different scales. Example: comparing variability of tumour volume (cm³) to PSA levels (ng/mL).

questions.stem: Which test should be used to compare pain scores (ordinal scale 0–10) between two independent groups?
questions.explanation: Pain score is ordinal. For ordinal data comparing two independent groups, use Mann-Whitney U test (non-parametric). An independent t-test would be inappropriate unless the scores are treated as continuous and are normally distributed.

questions.stem: A researcher wants to test whether there is an association between smoking (yes/no) and lung cancer (yes/no). The appropriate test is:
questions.explanation: Both smoking and lung cancer are categorical (binary) variables. Chi-square test for independence is appropriate. If expected frequencies are small, use Fisher's exact test.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a parametric test?
questions.explanation: Parametric tests: t-test (independent, paired, one-sample), ANOVA, Pearson correlation. Non-parametric: Mann-Whitney, Wilcoxon, Kruskal-Wallis, Spearman, Friedman. Parametric tests assume specific distributional forms.

questions.stem: A study compares three different doses of a drug on mean blood pressure reduction. What is the appropriate test? What if normality is violated?
questions.correct_answer: If normally distributed with equal variances: one-way ANOVA, followed by post-hoc tests (e.g., Tukey HSD) if significant. If normality violated or small sample: Kruskal-Wallis test (non-parametric ANOVA).
questions.explanation: Three groups, continuous outcome. Always check distribution first. Report which post-hoc test was used if ANOVA is significant.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a suitable use of the t-distribution?
options: Calculating a CI for the mean when σ is unknown and n is small
Testing a hypothesis about the mean when σ is unknown
Calculating a CI for a proportion with n = 20
Comparing means of two independent groups with unequal variances (Welch's test)
Comparing paired measurements before and after treatment
questions.explanation: CIs for proportions use the normal distribution (with SE = √(p̂(1−p̂)/n)), not the t-distribution. The other options are appropriate uses of the t-distribution.

questions.stem: A 2 × 2 contingency table has expected frequencies: 4.2, 4.8, 5.8, 5.2. The appropriate test is:
questions.explanation: One expected frequency (4.2) is < 5, and since 25% (1 of 4) of expecteds are < 5, the chi-square approximation is unreliable. Fisher's exact test is preferred. The rule: ≤20% of expecteds < 5, none < 1.

questions.stem: In multiple linear regression, adjusted R² differs from R² because:
options: Adjusted R² is always larger than R²
Adjusted R² penalises for adding irrelevant predictors
Adjusted R² is calculated only on the test set
Adjusted R² uses a different formula for the outcome
Adjusted R² requires normally distributed predictors
questions.explanation: Adjusted R² = 1 − (1 − R²)(n−1)/(n−k−1). It penalises for the number of predictors (k). Adding irrelevant predictors may increase R² but decrease adjusted R². This helps prevent overfitting.

questions.stem: The value that appears most frequently in a dataset is the:
questions.explanation: Mode = most frequent value. It is the only measure of central tendency that can be used for nominal categorical data (e.g., most common blood group).

questions.stem: What does 1 − β represent in hypothesis testing?
questions.correct_answer: 1 − β = Power = probability of correctly rejecting H₀ when it is false (i.e., detecting a true effect). β = Type II error probability (false negative).

questions.stem: In a randomised trial with a continuous outcome and baseline measurement, the most efficient analysis is:
options: Paired t-test on within-group change scores
questions.explanation: ANCOVA (analysis of covariance) with baseline as covariate is the most efficient (highest power) for analysing continuous outcomes in RCTs with baseline measures. It adjusts for baseline differences and reduces residual variance more than change scores or post-treatment only analysis.
questions.source_topic_reference: FRCR Medical Statistics — Clinical Trial Design

questions.stem: What is the difference between a confidence interval and a prediction interval?
questions.correct_answer: A CI gives the range of plausible values for a POPULATION PARAMETER (e.g., mean). A prediction interval gives the range within which a FUTURE INDIVIDUAL OBSERVATION is expected to fall. Prediction intervals are always wider than CIs because they include both parameter uncertainty and individual variability.
questions.explanation: For a new patient: 'What is the expected survival time?' → prediction interval (wider). For the trial: 'What is the mean survival in the population?' → confidence interval (narrower).

questions.stem: Which diagnostic measure is independent of disease prevalence?
options: All of the above depend on prevalence
questions.explanation: Sensitivity, specificity, and likelihood ratios (LR+, LR−) are intrinsic properties of the test and do NOT depend on prevalence. PPV and NPV are strongly influenced by prevalence. This is why LR+ is preferred for combining test results across different populations.

questions.stem: Missing data that is related to the outcome (e.g., sicker patients more likely to drop out) is called:
questions.explanation: MNAR: the probability of missingness depends on the unobserved outcome itself. MCAR: missingness is random. MAR: missingness depends on observed data. MNAR is the most problematic — analyses may be biased. Multiple imputation can help under MAR, but not MNAR.

questions.stem: A study randomises 100 patients (50 per group) and 10 in the treatment group cross over to control. Which method gives an unbiased estimate of treatment effectiveness?
questions.explanation: ITT (analyse as randomised) gives an unbiased estimate of the effect of ASSIGNING treatment (effectiveness in practice), but dilutes the effect due to crossover. Instrumental variable analysis can correct for non-compliance to estimate the effect of RECEIVING treatment. Per-protocol and as-treated are biased.
questions.source_topic_reference: FRCR Medical Statistics — Clinical Trial Design

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a type of data that can be ranked but has unequal intervals?
questions.explanation: Ordinal data: ordered categories with unequal intervals. Examples: ECOG performance status (0–4), Likert scales (1–5), AJCC stage (I–IV). The order matters but the distances between categories are not equal.

questions.stem: What is the I² statistic in meta-analysis and what does I² = 75% indicate?
questions.correct_answer: I² quantifies heterogeneity between studies in a meta-analysis. It describes the percentage of total variation across studies due to true heterogeneity rather than chance. I² = 75% indicates substantial heterogeneity. Values: 0–25% low, 25–50% moderate, 50–75% high, 75–100% very high. High I² suggests caution in pooling results — consider random-effects model or exploring sources of heterogeneity.
questions.explanation: Cochrane Handbook: I² > 50% may represent substantial heterogeneity. A random-effects model is more appropriate when heterogeneity is present.

questions.stem: The null hypothesis for a two-sample t-test is:
options: The two sample means are different
The two population means are equal
The two sample variances are equal
The two populations are normally distributed
The mean difference is greater than zero
questions.explanation: H₀: μ₁ = μ₂ (the population means are equal). H₁: μ₁ ≠ μ₂ (two-tailed). The t-test provides evidence against H₀. If p < 0.05, we reject H₀ and conclude the means differ.

questions.stem: In a study with n = 15 per group, an independent t-test shows p = 0.06. The most appropriate conclusion is:
options: The study is underpowered to detect the true effect
There is insufficient evidence to reject H₀ at the 0.05 level
The effect size is clinically unimportant
A non-parametric test should have been used
questions.explanation: p = 0.06 > 0.05 → not statistically significant. This does NOT prove 'no effect' (Type II error possible). It does not necessarily mean underpowered. It does not speak to clinical importance. Non-parametric test may have even less power.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a method for handling missing data?
questions.explanation: Bonferroni correction is for multiple comparison adjustment, not missing data. Methods for missing data: complete case (discard incomplete cases), LOCF (carry last value forward — generally NOT recommended), multiple imputation (gold standard, creates multiple complete datasets), maximum likelihood (uses all available data).

questions.stem: A study measures tumour size at baseline and after treatment in the same patients. The appropriate test to compare pre- and post-treatment values is:
questions.explanation: Before/after measurements on the same subjects are paired data. The paired t-test (or Wilcoxon signed-rank test if non-normal) accounts for the correlation between paired observations, giving greater power than an independent test.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a per-protocol and as-treated analysis?
questions.correct_answer: Per-protocol: analyse only patients who completed the study as per protocol (no major violations). As-treated: analyse patients based on the treatment they actually received, regardless of random assignment. Both are susceptible to selection bias (patients who complete/comply differ systematically from those who don't). ITT is the preferred primary analysis.
questions.source_topic_reference: FRCR Medical Statistics — Clinical Trial Design

questions.stem: What is the difference between descriptive and inferential statistics?
questions.correct_answer: Descriptive statistics summarise data (mean, median, SD, charts). Inferential statistics draw conclusions about populations from samples (hypothesis tests, CIs, regression). Descriptive statistics describe what was observed; inferential statistics make probabilistic statements about the wider population.

questions.stem: In a Kaplan-Meier survival curve, the vertical drop at an event time is proportional to:
options: The number of events at that time divided by the number at risk
The total number of events divided by the total sample size
The hazard rate at that time
The number of patients lost to follow-up
questions.explanation: At each event time tᵢ, S(t) drops by a factor of (nᵢ − dᵢ)/nᵢ, where nᵢ = number at risk just before tᵢ and dᵢ = number of events at tᵢ. Larger drops = more events relative to the at-risk population.

questions.stem: A diagnostic test has sensitivity 85% and specificity 90% in a population with 10% prevalence. The test result is positive. Calculate post-test probability of disease.
questions.correct_answer: Pre-test odds = 0.10/0.90 = 0.111. LR+ = 0.85/(1−0.90) = 0.85/0.10 = 8.5. Post-test odds = 0.111 × 8.5 = 0.944. Post-test probability = 0.944/(1+0.944) = 0.486 ≈ 49%. A positive test increases probability from 10% to ~49%.
questions.explanation: Bayes' theorem in diagnostic testing: LR+ updates pre-test to post-test probability. This test has moderate diagnostic value (LR+ = 8.5).

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a fixed-effect model in meta-analysis?
options: Assumes all studies estimate the same true effect
Allows study effects to vary around a distribution
Includes both within-study and between-study variance
Is also called the DerSimonian-Laird method
questions.explanation: Fixed-effect: all studies estimate the same true effect (only within-study variation). Random-effects: studies estimate different but related effects (includes both within and between-study variance). Random-effects is more conservative (wider CI) and appropriate when heterogeneity may be present.

questions.stem: Which is an example of stratified sampling?
options: Selecting every 10th patient from a list
Dividing the population into age groups and sampling proportionally from each
Selecting patients who are easiest to recruit
Giving all participants the same questionnaire
Randomly assigning patients to treatment groups
questions.explanation: Stratified sampling: population divided into strata (e.g., age groups, hospital sites), then random samples drawn from each stratum. Ensures representation of all subgroups. Systematic sampling: every kth patient. Convenience sampling: easy-to-recruit patients.

questions.stem: Calculate the mean and median of: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 14, 18.
questions.correct_answer: Mean = (2+3+5+7+11+14+18)/7 = 60/7 = 8.57. Median = 7 (4th of 7 ordered values). Mean > median suggests slight positive skew.
questions.explanation: Mean is the arithmetic average; median is the middle value. Comparing mean and median can indicate skewness direction.

questions.stem: What is the advantage of using multiple imputation over complete case analysis for missing data?
options: Multiple imputation is simpler to perform
Complete case analysis always gives biased results
Multiple imputation uses all available data and produces valid standard errors under MAR
Complete case analysis can only be done with large samples
Multiple imputation does not require any assumptions
questions.explanation: Multiple imputation: creates m complete datasets (typically m = 5–20), analyses each, pools results using Rubin's rules. This uses all available data and produces valid SEs under MAR. Complete case analysis discards incomplete cases — valid only under MCAR, inefficient.

questions.stem: What is the relationship between sample size, standard error, and confidence interval width?
questions.correct_answer: SE = SD/√n. As n increases, SE decreases. CI width = 2 × critical value × SE. So as n increases, both SE and CI width decrease. Precision improves with larger samples, but diminishing returns: quadrupling n halves the CI width.

questions.stem: The Durbin-Watson test checks for:
questions.explanation: Durbin-Watson tests for autocorrelation in regression residuals (assumption of independence). Values near 2 = no autocorrelation. < 1 or > 3 = concerning. Common in time series data (e.g., repeated measures).

questions.stem: Which of the following is the BEST approach when proportional hazards assumption is violated?
options: Use logistic regression at a fixed time point
Convert the outcome to binary and use chi-square
questions.explanation: When proportional hazards is violated, stratified Cox regression (stratifying by the violating variable) or Cox with time-dependent covariates are appropriate. Log-rank test also assumes proportional hazards. Landmark analysis (logistic at fixed time) wastes data.

questions.stem: In the LQ model for fractionated radiotherapy, BED (Biological Effective Dose) is calculated using which parameter?
questions.explanation: BED = nd × (1 + d/(α/β)). The α/β ratio characterises tissue sensitivity to fraction size. This radiobiological formula uses statistical concepts applied to clinical dose-response modelling.

questions.stem: If a test has 100% sensitivity, what does a negative result mean?
questions.correct_answer: 100% sensitivity means the test correctly identifies ALL diseased patients (no false negatives). Therefore, a NEGATIVE result definitively RULES OUT disease (SnNOut). However, specificity may be lower, so a positive result may not confirm disease.
questions.explanation: SnNOut rule: a highly Sensitive test rules OUT disease when negative. SpPIn: a highly Specific test rules IN disease when positive.

questions.stem: The Levene test checks which assumption?
questions.explanation: Levene's test checks homogeneity of variances (homoscedasticity). It tests H₀: variances are equal across groups. If p < 0.05, variances differ significantly → use Welch's ANOVA or non-parametric alternative.

questions.stem: A p-value of 0.03 means:
options: There is a 3% probability the null hypothesis is true
There is a 3% probability of observing the data (or more extreme) if H₀ is true
The Type II error rate is 3%
There is a 97% chance the alternative hypothesis is true
questions.explanation: p = P(data or more extreme | H₀). p = 0.03 < 0.05 → statistically significant. But this says NOTHING about clinical significance or the probability that H₀ is true.

questions.stem: What is the relationship between a two-sided 95% CI and a two-sided hypothesis test at α = 0.05?
questions.correct_answer: They are equivalent: if the 95% CI excludes the null value, p < 0.05. If the CI includes the null value, p > 0.05. The CI additionally shows the range of plausible effect sizes.

questions.stem: The assumption of 'non-informative censoring' in survival analysis means:
options: Censored patients have the same prognosis as those who remain
Censoring only occurs at random times
Censoring is independent of the event of interest
questions.explanation: Non-informative censoring: censored patients have the same future risk of the event as patients who remain under follow-up. In other words, censoring is independent of prognosis. This is a key assumption for valid KM and Cox analyses.

questions.stem: You want to compare the median survival time between two treatment groups. Which test is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: For comparing survival times accounting for censoring, the log-rank test is most appropriate. Mann-Whitney U cannot handle censored data appropriately. The log-rank test compares the entire survival distribution, not just medians.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a forest plot and a funnel plot?
questions.correct_answer: Forest plot: displays individual study effect sizes and CIs, with pooled estimate at the bottom. Used to visualise meta-analysis results. Funnel plot: plots effect size against precision (SE). Used to detect publication bias — asymmetry suggests missing studies (usually small negative studies).

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a measure of spread?
questions.explanation: Median is a measure of central tendency (location), not spread. Range, IQR, variance, and SD are all measures of spread (dispersion).

questions.stem: A study reports OR = 2.5 (95% CI: 1.3–4.8) for smoking and lung cancer. This means:
options: Smokers have 2.5 times the odds of lung cancer compared to non-smokers
Smokers have 2.5 times the risk of lung cancer compared to non-smokers
The result is not statistically significant
150% of smokers will develop lung cancer
questions.explanation: OR = 2.5 means the odds of lung cancer in smokers is 2.5× the odds in non-smokers. The CI (1.3–4.8) excludes 1, so p < 0.05. We cannot say 'risk' (RR) without baseline risk. The direction is smoking → lung cancer, not reverse.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a cohort study design?
options: Comparing current smokers to former smokers and following them for disease development
Interviewing lung cancer patients about past smoking habits
Measuring smoking prevalence in a cross-sectional survey
Randomising patients to smoking cessation vs usual care
Analysing hospital records of lung cancer patients
questions.explanation: Cohort study: groups defined by EXPOSURE (smoking status), followed forward for OUTCOME (disease development). Case-control: groups defined by OUTCOME (disease), looking backward at EXPOSURE. RCT: random allocation to exposure.

questions.stem: Hosmer-Lemeshow test is used to assess:
options: Goodness-of-fit of a logistic regression model
Proportional hazards assumption in Cox regression
Normality of residuals in linear regression
questions.explanation: Hosmer-Lemeshow test assesses goodness-of-fit of logistic regression by comparing observed vs predicted frequencies across deciles of predicted risk. Non-significant p-value (p > 0.05) indicates adequate fit. However, it has low power and alternative measures (AIC, pseudo-R²) are also used.

questions.stem: What is the difference between an observational study and an experimental study?
questions.correct_answer: Observational: investigator observes outcomes without intervening. Examples: cohort, case-control, cross-sectional. May show association but cannot prove causation. Experimental: investigator assigns exposure (e.g., treatment). RCT is the gold standard experimental design. Randomisation controls confounding.

questions.stem: A cross-sectional study measures both exposure and outcome at the same time. Its main limitation is:
options: Cannot establish temporal sequence (cause before effect)
Cannot be used for hypothesis generation
Is more expensive than an RCT
questions.explanation: Cross-sectional studies measure exposure and outcome simultaneously, so they cannot determine which came first. They can estimate prevalence and generate hypotheses, but cannot establish causality. Example: finding an association between grey hair and heart disease — does grey hair cause heart disease or do they share a common cause (age)?

questions.stem: Bar charts are most appropriate for displaying:
options: The distribution of a continuous variable
The relationship between two continuous variables
The trend in a variable over time
questions.explanation: Bar charts display categorical data (or continuous data grouped by category). Histograms show distribution of a continuous variable. Scatter plots show relationships between two continuous variables. Survival curves (KM plots) show survival over time.

questions.stem: You have data on 5-year survival (yes/no) and want to model the probability of survival adjusting for age, sex, and tumour stage. Which model is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Survival at a fixed time point (5 years) as binary outcome → logistic regression. If the time-to-event was available (not just binary), Cox regression would be more powerful as it uses all survival time information and handles censoring.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a histogram and a bar chart?
questions.correct_answer: Histogram: used for continuous data. Bars touch each other (continuous scale). X-axis represents class intervals. Bar chart: used for categorical data. Bars have gaps. The bars can be reordered (no inherent order for nominal data).

questions.stem: A box plot displays all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Box plot typically shows: median (middle line), IQR (box), whiskers (range or 1.5×IQR), and outliers (points). Mean is NOT typically shown on a standard box plot, though some variations include it.
